James Kirkup is a former Executive Editor (Politics) for The Telegraph and was a lobby journalist for 16 years. James has a particular interest in subjects including economics and defence. Before joining The Telegraph he was Political Editor of The Scotsman, covered European politics and economics for Bloomberg, and reported from countries including Iran, Zimbabwe and the USA.

            James Kirkup
        
    

            
    

        
            Columnist
        

        
    

            
    
        
            
                Show biography
                
                    
                
            
        
    

        

        
            
    
    
        
	
		
	

    

        
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
        James Kirkup is a former Executive Editor (Politics) for The Telegraph and was a lobby journalist for 16 years. James has a particular interest in subjects including economics and defence. Before joining The Telegraph he was Political Editor of The Scotsman, covered European politics and economics for Bloomberg, and reported from countries including Iran, Zimbabwe and the USA.

Should Britain charge EU students less for their university tuition? The question that bedevils Andy Burnham’s European reset is the wrong one to ask.

The right one: why does it matter so much? The answer – because years of failure left our higher education sector to drift into the AI era dangerously unreformed and recklessly dependent on foreign students’ fees – raises another question. How many of our universities will survive what comes next?

Whatever its flaws, and no matter how strongly some people feel about “Mickey Mouse” degrees and the need for skilled trades, the higher education sector is important to Britain. The sector educates almost three million people, employs 400,000 more and accounts for more than £250bn of economic activity.

Our universities educate doctors, engineers and scientists, conduct world-leading research and help create the businesses on which growth depends. If you haven’t heard of Fractile yet, you will. It’s a Bristol-based AI chip designer that emerged from Oxford University just four years ago and is valued at more than £5bn today.

Universities are also major local employers. In many towns and cities, they support thousands of jobs directly and through student spending and local supply chains.

We can’t afford to let higher education fail. But nor can we preserve every university unchanged.

Vice chancellors are correct when they say that they cannot afford to educate Europeans for less money. That’s because for years successive governments refused to let domestic tuition fees keep pace with inflation, preferring to avoid the pain of asking students to pay more. The result was a steady erosion of university finances.

Universities responded by recruiting more international students, whose fees are uncapped. According to the Social Market Foundation, international students generate a surplus of 31p for every pound spent teaching them. Domestic students produce a net loss of 8p.

Students and staff strike over budget cuts at Edinburgh University
			
		

		
		
			
				
				    Credit: Getty/Jeff J Mitchell
			   
			
		
	



	

	
	









  
  

	

	
	

	
	



  
  
    Foreign students subsidising British students has created uncomfortable dependencies. Some of our highest-ranked universities rely heavily on Chinese students, leaving them exposed to decisions made in Beijing. Others depend on recruitment from India, Nigeria and elsewhere. All are vulnerable to immigration policy and international competition.

University leaders themselves cannot escape responsibility, however. Some institutions borrowed heavily to finance expansion, with some running up debts exceeding their annual income. Others expanded student numbers without matching investment in teaching staff or accommodation.

The consequences are becoming impossible to ignore. In May, the Commons education committee warned that university insolvencies are now a real possibility, with grim consequences for students, staff and local economies. The Labour-majority committee also found that the Government had no clear plan for dealing with a university collapse.

The mortal risk facing universities isn’t purely down to financial management. Governments have also failed to use their leverage to demand fundamental changes in what universities offer.

For decades, higher education has largely meant leaving home at 18 to study for three years then entering the labour market. As universities expanded, the world changed around them, yet their basic product remained much the same. That is a missed opportunity, and a recipe for trouble.

Prof Tim Blackman, the former vice-chancellor of the Open University, argues that the traditional honours degree was designed for a small elite, but expanded to mass higher education without anyone reconsidering whether it remained the best approach.

Blackman convincingly argues for more shorter courses. It would allow people to accumulate qualifications throughout their working lives rather than completing their education in their early 20s then embarking on careers that could last 50 years. Why spend three years acquiring knowledge that may become outdated within a decade? Why not study for shorter qualifications, enter employment and return when new skills are needed?

Traditional degrees will remain essential in medicine, engineering and other disciplines. And residential education offers benefits beyond academic instruction. But a system serving millions should offer more variety.

Growing public doubts about higher education fuel the case for change. The latest British Social Attitudes survey found that 42 per cent believe Britain has too many graduates. More than a third think a degree is not worth the time and money.

Many families see higher education as a story of young people being loaded with debts for qualifications that do not always deliver the expected careers or earnings. Yet only 18 per cent favour reducing opportunities to attend university.

The answer is neither to defend every course nor dismiss higher education as a waste of money. It is to offer more choice, better value and qualifications that meet changing needs. The advent of AI makes this case burningly urgent.

AI is transforming learning and assessment, changing employers’ requirements and raising razor-edged questions about the value of a degree. Universities should lead this revolution. Some are. But institutions struggling to balance their books and maintain existing courses are in no position to reinvent post-18 education for a new economic era.

A paper for the Higher Education Policy Institute, published this summer by Prof Sir Chris Husbands, makes sobering reading here.

Husbands, the former vice-chancellor of Sheffield Hallam University, argues that financial pressures have arrived faster than expected, compounded by AI, changing student expectations and declining public confidence. He concludes that existing institutional arrangements are unsustainable.

Instead of the one-size-fits-all status quo, he envisages globally competitive research universities, regional institutions, specialist providers and partnerships with further education. He also calls for arrangements allowing universities to merge or close.

Ministers may be beginning to contemplate differentiation between universities, accepting that some should be supported and others subjected to tougher conditions.

Buried in the recent Budget was a significant decision about graduate visas. Graduates of universities with strong labour-market outcomes and high immigration compliance will retain the ability to offer two-year visas to graduates. Lesser institutions will be able to offer only 18 months.

The criteria remain undefined, but the principle matters. Universities will receive different treatment according to their performance, potentially affecting their ability to recruit lucrative international students.

The prospect of a two-tier system horrifies some universities, but more fundamentally, it raises a question governments have long avoided: should every existing university survive in its present form?

The answer cannot automatically be yes. Higher education exists to educate students, advance knowledge and serve society, not guarantee the survival of an institution or business model.

The EU fees row is just the beginning of a hard conversation. Britain needs excellent universities and flexible education for an economy being transformed by AI. That will require more money in some places, radical reform in others, and the acceptance that some universities will shrink or merge. Others will simply cease to exist.
